drapeaux.note: The English phrase “nowhere to be found in Buridan's writings” is the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's own wording, checked verbatim on the page (Zupko, “John Buridan,” plato.stanford.edu/entries/buridan/: “This particular example is nowhere to be found in Buridan's writings”). The same sentence in the body (“nowhere to be found in his writings”) renders the French “introuvable dans ses écrits” and is not presented as verbatim.

accroche: A donkey starves between two identical piles of hay. Buridan never wrote this story.
contenu_vulgarise:
A donkey stands at an equal distance from two piles of hay, identical in every respect. Nothing pushes it to prefer one over the other. Unable to choose, it stays motionless, and starves between the two. The story has carried for centuries the name of Jean Buridan, a 14th-century French philosopher and logician, rector of the University of Paris. It serves as an easy jibe against his theory of free will: if the will truly needs a reason to choose, a choice between two perfectly equal options should be impossible.

There is a problem: the donkey appears in no known text by Buridan.

## A Story Older Than Its Name

The article that the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy devotes to him is categorical: the fable is “nowhere to be found in his writings.” Its best hypothesis is that it was born as a parody, invented by later critics to ridicule a doctrine they judged absurd, that one can remain free by simply remaining inactive.

The scenario itself is far older than Buridan. Aristotle already reports it in his treatise *On the Heavens*, in the 4th century BCE, in order to refute it: he describes a man at an equal distance from food and drink, equally hungry and thirsty, equally bound to each extreme, and who for that reason necessarily stays where he is. Aristotle attributes this argument to Anaximander, two centuries earlier still, who used it to explain why the Earth stays motionless at the center of the world: at an equal distance from all points, it would have no reason to move in one direction rather than another.

## What Buridan Actually Wrote

His real position, in his *Questions on the Nicomachean Ethics*, is more measured than the fable lets on. He holds that the will can suspend its choice when the good of each option remains uncertain: provided that the intellect judges that it is preferable to examine the question further before deciding. Suspending is not being stuck: it is still a choice, the choice to wait.

## What This Shifts

The story has crossed almost two thousand five hundred years while changing bearer and meaning three times: a cosmological argument for Anaximander, a refuted objection for Aristotle, a spiteful caricature hung on the name of a logician who never wrote it. Each generation saw in it proof of what it already wanted to demonstrate. The name that remains is not that of the author, but that of the most convenient target.

carte.punch: Buridan's ass starves between two piles of hay. Buridan never wrote this story.
carte.idee: The fable attributed to the medieval philosopher Jean Buridan is nowhere to be found in his writings, according to the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. The scenario actually goes back to Aristotle, who reports it in order to refute it, and to Anaximander before him.

quiz.question: What does the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's inquiry reveal about “Buridan's ass”?
choix: Buridan does describe this example, but in a theology treatise rather than a logic one
Buridan borrowed this example directly from Aristotle, who reports it in On the Heavens
The donkey example is nowhere to be found in Buridan's writings, probably born of a parody
The example is authentic in Buridan but mistranslated in modern editions
quiz.explication: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy article is explicit: this example is found nowhere in Buridan's writings. It puts forward as its best explanation a parody, invented by critics to ridicule his theory of free will: it is neither a direct borrowing from Aristotle, nor a mistranslated passage, nor an authentic text misplaced in another treatise.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the text, to whom does Aristotle attribute the argument of the indifference scenario, taken up in On the Heavens?
choix: Jean Buridan, who would have developed it a century earlier
Jack Zupko, in his article on Buridan for the Stanford Encyclopedia
Anaximander, who used it to explain the immobility of the Earth
Plato, in a passage of the Phaedo devoted to rational choice
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Aristotle reports this argument in On the Heavens, attributing it to Anaximander, two centuries before him, who used it to explain why the Earth stays motionless at the center of the world.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is Buridan's real position on the choice between two uncertain options, according to his Questions on the Nicomachean Ethics?
choix: The will must choose immediately, even when the good of each option remains uncertain
The will can suspend its choice to examine the options better, which remains a choice
Only an outside judge can decide between two options whose good is uncertain
A choice between two equal options is impossible, as the fable of the donkey says
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Buridan holds that suspending an uncertain choice, in order to examine it further, remains a choice, the choice to wait, which is more measured than the caricature of the fable.
